sections.heading: The idea
sections.body_md:
Single-ended amplifiers treat every disturbance on their input as signal. A **differential** circuit processes the difference between two inputs. Noise coupled equally onto both lines, supply ripple and ground bounce are largely **common-mode**, so they cancel in the difference. Differential stages also make DC coupling between stages easier, because bias levels can be matched on both sides.

The workhorse is the **source-coupled pair**. Two matched transistors have their sources tied to a single tail current source, and each has its own drain load. The tail fixes the sum of the two drain currents; the inputs decide how it splits. Balanced, each side carries half. Driving one gate while holding the other shows how the pair works. The driven device acts like a follower into the shared source, and the other device sees that as a common-gate input. The two drains therefore move by equal and opposite amounts. A pure common-mode input changes neither current when the tail is ideal, so the outputs stay still.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
\[ I_{D1} + I_{D2} = I_{SS}, \qquad I_{D1} = I_{D2} = \tfrac12I_{SS} \ (\text{balanced}) \]
\[ \left|\frac{v_{od}}{v_{id}}\right| = g_mR_D, \qquad \left|\frac{v_{o1}}{v_{id}}\right| = \frac{g_mR_D}2 \]

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md: A pair with a 0.6 mA tail, \(R_D = 4\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and a 2.5 V supply sits at \(2.5 - 0.3(4) = 1.3\ \mathrm{V}\) on each drain. If each device has \(g_m = 1.5\ \mathrm{mS}\), a 20 mV differential input produces 120 mV between the drains and 60 mV at either drain alone.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md:
- Giving each side the full tail current at balance.
- Expecting a common-mode input to move the outputs when the tail is ideal.
- Forgetting that a single-ended output gets only half the differential gain.
